hypothesis: Compared with the measured 256-thread, four-accumulator fused mapping, 128-thread CTAs can retain the same 256-float tile boundaries by assigning two adjacent floats to each lane. An aligned float2 path may reduce load instruction overhead, while a scalar fallback preserves correctness for 4-byte-aligned inputs and an explicit odd-element path handles tails. Keeping 1024 CTAs/partials and the 256-thread finalizer fixed makes this a contrasting within-CTA mapping experiment; its effect on full-call time and the FP64 error bound remains for controller measurement.
notes: The supplied current source uses a materialized absolute-value pass and atomic reduction, so this candidate uses the two-stage fused topology represented by the measured prior source while changing the CTA mapping. It preserves 1024 CTAs, 256 input elements per CTA tile, 1024 partials, and the existing 256-thread CUB finalizer. The candidate is unmeasured; correctness, required sizes, error bound, and full-call time are left to the controller.
transformations: Use a fused input absolute-sum and CTA-local reduction in the first kernel, then reduce 1024 partials in the existing one-CTA, 256-thread finalizer.
Use 1024 input CTAs with 128 threads each; assign two adjacent floats per lane so each CTA retains its 256-float tile and original grid-stride tile boundaries.
Load pairs through float2 only when the input pointer is 8-byte aligned; use scalar pair loads otherwise and explicitly assign an odd final element to its owning lane.
Keep all partial writes and the final output write unconditional for each call; leave official correctness and full-call measurement to the controller.
